utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, you told us yesterday that you're of Serbian nationality. You were born in Banja Luka, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were your parents of Serbian nationality too?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother is a Serb from Banja Luka and my father is a Serbian, I mean from Serbia itself, Krusevac. So yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not get any translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you had a passport showing that you were a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also a passport showing that you were a citizen of Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us in what capacity you demanded this passport and how you obtained it, since you are a Serb and you live in Bosnia and Herzegovina and you live in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son is also a Serb, and he was issued a passport because he was the secretary of the basketball club. They had their matches in Split and Rijeka. And I had only a Bosnian passport, and it is very difficult for me to transport it, but when I accepted to be a witness for the Defence, the only way I could do that was to get the passport. But there are Serbs in our case who were issued passports of Croatia; not all of them, but some of them did get Croatian passports; and Croats, yes, they all got them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you properly, you received this passport only to be able to come and testify here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got that passport to be able to use it, because with that passport I could also go to visit Montenegro to see my daughter, via Dubrovnik, via Herceg-Novi, and with it I also went to see relatives in Pula. So I used it not only to come here, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to give reasons to show that you had connections or links with Croatia to be able to get the passport?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only reason perhaps was that I lived in Vitez, which is Central Bosnia, and that I testified here. And the reason my son was given it was, as I have said, so that he could travel with the basketball team. So he was issued a passport in 1994, 1995. So there wasn't a problem. Perhaps even if I did not apply for it to go to The Hague, after all, I've lived in Vitez for 43 years, and I told you yesterday all that I did there. People know me. I do not have any political blemishes, so perhaps that was the reason why I was issued that passport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As somebody living in Vitez, of Serbian origin, living in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is easy to get a passport from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is how I got it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now, today, a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none. Once I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, but after that I did not join any party, nor did I accept any of the parties: the HDZ, SDP, or whatever. That is, politically I am quite uncommitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you carried out political functions, because I think that you were the mayor of Vitez in 1984, 1985. At the time you did represent a political party, the League of Communists, the one you mentioned just now?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've told us that you no longer belong to any party. Could you tell us when you stopped belonging to a political party?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, when the 14th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia took place in Belgrade, I was so disappointed by the whole congress and by the split, by the schism in the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and I could not really feel I could belong any longer to such a disintegrated League of Communists, so that I requested to leave. And I was too disenchanted, too disappointed by those groups, by those leading cliques, as we would call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment ago you told us that you didn't belong to any political party; for instance, you don't belong to the HDZ. But could you tell us in a few words what the programme of that party is, what its positions are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think, Mr. Lopez-Terres, we need that now. Could I ask you to bear in mind that we are under pressure of time this week, I'm afraid. I notice the witness took about three quarters of an hour in chief, and I would ask you to try and restrict yourself to that time, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in Vitez during the war. You therefore experienced how the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was created and then how the Croatian Republic was created in 1993. How did you yourself experience the creation of these various institutions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that, as I have already said, I did not belong to any party. I had no role in all this. And all these things came into being without any -- without myself playing a part in that. The only influence, political, which I can have is to vote or not to vote for HDZ or SDP or SDA. That is the only political role that I can have now. However, my opinion now -- and that is irrespective of a party which might have been in power -- such a crazy, such an insane -- I do not have any other word for it -- such an insane conflict. Because Vitez was the front line. All the villages were criss-crossed with those trenches, there was gunfire all over, blockades and all sorts of things, and you couldn't really have any proper political power that would have been up to expectations of the majority of the population, because unfortunately that kind of policy had done its harm. It led to the division, to the ethnic division -- Muslims, Croats, Serbs -- and so on and so forth. But when it calmed down, when the International Community came there and its institutions, the relations began to improve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Mr. Lukovic. You thought that the creation of the three institutions was justified at the time, did you? Can you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. answer with a yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what, I don't like it because it is as if participating in a quiz; it is so difficult to say yes or no. I was not for the separation of anyone. I liked the Yugoslavia as it was, except that in that Yugoslavia I did not like the leadership which pursued a policy which did not meet the interests of all the peoples. And Bosnia is a very curious place because it is mixed ethnically in terms of religion and in every other respect. So that it's easiest for us to live when we live together, because we've spent centuries living together. I do not think that anyone is happy now after this division; that is what I think. And now we're trying to get used to each other again. So that I never applauded any government or any division; I do not like that division in Bosnia into the Federation of Republika Srpska. But who am I to decide about how a state will be constituted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that your son was part of the HVO forces. He was even wounded, wasn't he, during the war. Could you tell us which unit he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the unit, but he was with the HVO, the Croat Defence Counsel, the military wing of the HVO. Now, whether it was a brigade and whether it had a name, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not in a position to tell us whether he was part of the Vitez Brigade, for instance, which was commanded by Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I think so, because, yes, it was a brigade from Vitez, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was he wounded, and where was he wounded?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wounded at Bobasi, I think it could have been December, and he was wounded in the arm. Members of the BH army had attacked in that area, and he was wounded there and spent about a month on sick-leave. May I add something, if I may?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you know we're under time pressure and I'd like us to move forward. You told us that in June 1993 you received a summons from the defence administration in Vitez, the one which was from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, from the HVO, and you agreed to answer the summons, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get the summons from the national defence administration. It was an oral information, a request from a member of the military police who had a list of sorts. He asked me about my name and I told him that I was Dusan Lukovic, and then he said, "You are to report to the town library." So I really do not know if the list was drawn by the defence administration or not, or the defence office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the representatives of the HVO military police provided you with this information, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they informed me about it and requested that I report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time there were somehow two parallel authorities, weren't there, in the area. What would your reaction have been if you had received a similar summons from the BH army, from the Muslims? Would you have agreed to going and digging trenches also for the BH army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is in the affirmative. I told you yesterday that I agreed to do it because it was regulated by law, and I was a military conscript. So had I been in Mahala and received such summons, as a Serb I would have gone to dig this. With all this war predicament, I thought, well, if I go there and dig those trenches, we shall protect the lives of those young people, and then when the UN arrives, they will sit around a big table and put an end to this crazy war. So I would have, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a law or an act because of which you were mobilised. It was decided by the HVO, and it was under the decision of the Herceg-Bosna Community, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a decree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were sent to the work platoon, you told us that it was organised somehow and you mentioned people who were responsible for organising the work platoons. And you mentioned the Vinac brothers, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Marijan Vinac one of the people you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you that there were two of them. All I know is that it was a Vinac who drove a van or, rather, a minibus, when he took us to Zabrdje, to Zaselje. But whether his first name is Marijan, or the other one, I really don't know, even though I know both of them, I know their parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you know Marijan Vinac, son of Franjo.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in touch with them; I know them by sight. We also say hello to each other, because to them I'm Uncle Dusko. I am quite close with their parents, but I do not see them, I do not socialise with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We agree on this, don't we: Among the two people organising the work platoons, there was Marijan Vinac, son of Franjo.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really say yes or no because I don't know. But it was a Vinac who drove the minibus. There was a young man called Males who looked like a commander of the work platoon but only for Kolonija. Every locality formed work platoons. It started even at their own initiative, because one had to protect the village if, you know, there was any destruction, that one needed some help. So that even we who lived in the town went out to the front line to dig where and when it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Vinac family, they come from Donja Veceriska, do they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their mother lives there, and one of the brothers too. But both the brothers have houses in Vitez, below Gradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were mobilised to work in those work platoons for the first time in June 1993. Do you know whether there were similar work platoons in April 1993 in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, because the first time I went into the field was in June 1993. But I did see in places where I went through that there already were some trenches, either for men to stand in or to sit in. But the front line was not fixed. Perhaps they were dug by soldiers themselves when there was no fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I suppose these are just guesses of yours. You don't know who dug the trenches which you saw in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just guessing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1993, I believe you were still living in your apartment in Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Muslims living in Vitez but in that neighbourhood of Kolonija, whether they were arrested? Did you witness such people being arrested?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How shall I say? Arrested. You know, later on I talked to another colleague of mine who is also a sociologist, and another one with whom I worked in the factory with, and I know that they were put up at the Workers' University. Later on the situation was really very tense. There were many displaced people who had arrived from Jajce and who had also suffered at the Serbs' hands, so on and so forth. There was gunfire and war. My feeling was that Muslims, I mean Muslim men, were being put away, sheltered, in order to prevent crimes, because Muslim women had left. Had they been arresting Muslims, I mean men, they would have been arresting everybody. But I think this colleague of mine spent some five or seven days in the cinema of the Workers' University. But everything else is just stories, and of course one can always question the accuracy of stories. I want to talk only about what I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, some of your friends of Muslim nationality were -- well, you don't like the word "arrested," but they were detained in some premises in Vitez, and this was done by the HVO, starting on the 16th of April; do we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except that the wording should be different. I think those were not arrests, they were being taken in; and there is a difference, arresting somebody and taking somebody under your custody to shelter him. I do not know how some individuals treated Muslims, and that is something that I do not know. But they all left those places. I've heard from people, saying, "I was in a camp, I was in a detainee in a camp," and yet he's sitting in a cinema where you have armchairs. I mean, some Muslims were put away -- well, yes, perhaps you could call it -- some would call it arrested. But I think that there should have been a decision, that some court should have issued some decisions, but no court issued any decisions. They were simply put in the cinema for, I don't know, seven days or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Due process. But they were detained for some time by the HVO forces, and this happened in various locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Lopez-Terres. Could the witness be asked another question on this episode with the cinema? He told us that they were detained, that the Muslims were kept in the cinema. According to you, why were they kept there? What were the reasons for them being kept in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you my opinion. Because there was shooting all over the place and shelling, explosions throughout Vitez. I don't know who was in command and who was not, but what happened was that the Muslims were detained. They weren't arrested. That seems to me to be a strong term. But they were detained in those premises. And I think that that was done mostly to prevent even more bloodshed from taking place and to prevent those people from becoming victims. Because if individuals wanted to kill, say, a Muslim or a Serb or a Croat, there were people who had gone quite insane, quite crazy at that time, so it was very difficult to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. control anybody who had lost his nerve. And I think that that was the main reason, and probably the Muslims who were there said what it was like there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain it to us? I think you told us that they were detained for their own safety because there was a dangerous situation there. But if that was so, why, then, this did not apply to Croats as well? No Croat was detained, as far as I know, or kept in those safe places.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the general danger, we were all in danger from the shelling, shooting, and so on. But here they probably assessed -- and I can only assume that; I cannot claim it -- but there was the possibility that Croat -- of Croat ethnicity could attack a Muslim, abuse them, maltreat them, or something like that. Because there were many Croats who had come from Grahovcici, Brankovcici, Zenica, Jajce, and all those places, and our own people as well, whose children had lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, Mr. Lukovic, you are familiar with the Workers' University. You told us about it. You know also the school in Dubravica, you know the chess club, you know the SDK building, you know the veterinary station, and you know that dozens, hundreds of Muslims were taken there, to use your expression, were taken there in April. There were no Croats amongst them. There were only Muslims, men and women.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the places that you have just mentioned, I know them well, and I can say that that is true; that did exist. I heard that from the people who were there. But I once again would like to state that there was no need to detain Croats, who were the majority population compared to the Muslims. And if there was a settling of accounts between the Croats and Muslims, then it was very dangerous for Croats too. When the Mahala, for example, had a conflict like that take place, and they had to leave the Mahala. They withdrew too. So for every nationality who was in the minority found it difficult. The only thing that happened in Vitez was that the Serbs did not have --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a place where Croats were kept for reasons of security and detained there against their wish, like the Muslims that you told us about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if among those persons who were detained in places which we mentioned, some were also forced to dig trenches around the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that, and the people that I talked to, they didn't tell me that. They didn't say that they had been forced to dig. But when we went to the trenches, then there were Muslims there too who had been detained. And when they went home and when I went trench digging --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about April. I'm referring to April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. In order to get on, Mr. Lukovic, could you just concentrate on the questions? You were asked if you knew of any place in which the Croats were detained. Did you know of any such place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said no, I did not know of any such place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You did not make any audible response. We now have your reply. Now, you said something about when you were digging trenches, you came across Muslims who had been detained. Now, were they digging trenches too?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I went to dig trenches, together with me, from Vitez, the Muslims and Croats went too. They weren't detained. We were just mobilised and we went to dig the trenches, and we were there together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What about the Muslims who had been detained? Did you see any Muslims under guard at the trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only in June that I went to Zabrdje for the first time when the trench-digging went on, so about that part of April, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I mean, what I asked you was whether you saw any Muslims under guard digging trenches. Is the answer you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever I went to the localities where we dug trenches, there was not a single Muslim who was brought there under arms, nor were arms directed at them. Croats and Muslims and myself, we all had the same treatment: Zabrdje, Zaselje, and all the localities that we went to. The work platoons were multi-ethnic, so that -- and I have heard stories, for example, that there was a Muslim -- well, I don't know that Muslims dug alone. We all dug the trenches. And I can only assume that there should have been more younger Muslims, and they couldn't get arms on the Croatian side to go up to the line, whereas the Serbs that were there, like my son, they did have weapons. About 350 Serbs were included into the HVO, either in work platoons or as civil defence members or like my son and the other people who were the armed component of the HVO. And all of them were given treatment as soldiers of the HVO and all of them received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, you know that most of the Muslims, most Muslims left Vitez after the conflict in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do know. That's true. A lot of Muslims did leave. And I must also say that a number of Serbs, not a large number, but a number of Serbian families left Vitez as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those Muslims who left Vitez, did they do so of their own volition or were they forced to do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that in some cases they were forced to do so, and in other cases their psychological state was such that they wanted to leave the environment, just as there were Croats who left Vitez and went to Zagreb with their families, or to Split or wherever. Because it was difficult to live in Vitez, and extremely dangerous as well. However, I do believe that this was a problem of flats, of apartments too, accommodation, because the people who came didn't have anywhere to live. I heard stories going round of that kind that individuals would go around in the course of the night and perhaps threaten these people, "If you don't leave of your own free will, we'll make you leave." Perhaps there were telephone calls to that effect. And this created the general psychosis in which people wished to leave. And just one moment, please. May I just add that all the Muslims are coming back today and their apartments are being returned to them today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter about that now. Let us try and finish your evidence, please, Mr. Lukovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tell us that some of you -- that some of them were forced -- that some of them received threats from people who came by night, who wanted to take over their apartments, but those who were threatening them, they were Croats, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I heard rumours about this going round, so I cannot claim myself that it took place, as I can say for the work platoons, where I was personally. And I assume, with the passage of time, that cases like that could have existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You told us and confirmed it a while ago that the work platoon in which you worked was a multi-ethnic, and I should like to show you a document and to invite you to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a document which is Z1210.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document dated 21st of September, 1993. As you can see, it was issued by the defence office in Vitez, by the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, and you are the first on the list of 12 persons who were mobilised by this office. Do we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is your name under number 1 in a list of 12 mobilised persons. It is on the top of the page in the original.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to look at the first part of the document, where there is a list of 20 individuals, and that was evidently the work platoon called Sofa. Do you see that list?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I get the French interpretation, please? I cannot hear it. I'm getting English. I'm sorry. Yes. Now it's all right. Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These names, those 20 names, are they Serb names, Croat names, Muslim names? What are they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we have a problem with the interpretation. At times we hear English on the French channel. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now we do hear the French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We again have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we get something done about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see how we get on now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three. One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There's no problem with the English. Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were saying -- you were speaking about the ethnicity of people on this list. What are they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not getting the English. This has got to be sorted out. The registrar suggests that the wrong buttons are being pressed, but I don't know whether that's so or not. It's going now. Right. We'll try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew all these people, you were able to identify these people straight away as being of Romany origin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we better adjourn. Mr. Lopez-Terres, how much more do you have for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I only have one question, Your Honour. But, you know, there are so few opportunities for us to speak French in this Tribunal that I think we have to respect this principle, that I'm authorised to speak French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I agree. What we'll do is adjourn for ten minutes and try and get it sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna suggests we try for the last question. And here is the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The technical staff say it's working, so let's try again. Your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, yesterday you mentioned the very good relationship you had with the Cerkez family, with his parents, with himself. You spent holidays together, if I understood you properly. You got Mr. Cerkez into the SPS factory, and you were very pleased with the work he was doing. Now, how far do they go back, these good links with his family? Could you specify the time when you started having such connections?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that at the end of the 1960s, that is to say, from the 1970s onwards, it could have been 1970 when I graduated, I think that from that time on --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. I wanted to move more speedily. So you've had these connections with the Cerkez family already back in the 1960s. Here's my question: From 1992 more specifically, did you maintain those types of quality links with his family, and especially with him, Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have ties, links, and I would go to them for Christmas, for Easter, and so on. I remember when there was an attack on the 24th of December at Bobasi that I went to take a Christmas tree from his father and mother, because I wanted to decorate the Christmas tree for Christmas and for New Year for my own family. And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet Mario Cerkez at the time when he was the commander of the Vitez Brigade? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When I was at home, we would sit and have a chat with his father. He wasn't at the lines where I was. And I don't think he had time to talk to me either during that period, because the situation was very complex and he probably had a lot to do with the organisation of the defence, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, therefore, did not have any opportunity of speaking with the accused, Mario Cerkez, of the events. You couldn't speak with him about the war and the fighting, about everything that happened following April 1993.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was ill, then I talked to him. I was ill for 30 days and we had a talk then, but I didn't discuss the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukovic, we had some technical difficulties when we were discussing the document presented to you by the Prosecution, it is document Z1210.2, and your answers were not recorded. So for the record, could you give us your answer again, please? I'm going to ask you in the following way: On page 1 of the original text there is a list of 20 persons. Tell us, please, according to your own personal knowledge, what nationality were these individuals?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only number 2, Samir Besic, was -- I think there was a village called Besici, towards Kruscica. I think he was a Muslim. But all the rest, the Ramici, Suvalici, Fafulovici, Sejdici and all the others, they were all Romanies. We have a settlement of Romanies, and they always went to dig together. If there weren't 19 of them, there would be 10 of them, 11 of them, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that, Mr. Lukovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know those people because I was the mayor, I was an activist. I contacted them. And we say hello to each other today as well. And I went digging with them together. I know Fafulovic, Adil Fafulovic, for example, personally; he came to my building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. On page 2 of the original text there is another list of 12 people, and it says that these 12 people were mobilised for the work platoon. Under number 1 there is your name; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take a look at that list and tell the Trial Chamber and all of us here in the courtroom what the nationalities of these people are on that list?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Dusan Lukovic, a Serb; Dzevad Junuzovic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little slower, please, so we can record it.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1 is my name, I'm a Serb; then Junuzovic and Viteskic were Muslims; Babic and Barbic, Anto, Ivo, and all the rest, were Croats. I should like to mention that Mirsad Viteskic, after me, was the mayor of Vitez, he was the president of the municipality. And we dug in the same trench, the two Muslims and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was a sort of work platoon of former mayors. That was a little joke on my part.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we joked about that too while we were digging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukovic. The Prosecutor suggested in one of his questions that regulation with respect to work assignments and duties were brought by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. My question is the following: The regulations with respect to work duty and work platoons, did they exist in the former Yugoslavia, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina when it was a component part of the former Yugoslavia? Do you happen to know that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a law on national defence. There was a federal law and republican laws. And as far as I know later on, from the conversations I had, this was used by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well and the HVO too. I'm sure that the regulation was adapted, but it emanated from the law. And I think that the wording is the same or similar as it is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to refer to D103/2 and D104/2 which have been admitted into evidence and speak about this topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, when you were asked to explain how you think that, for their own safety, the Muslims were detained, as you said, in the Workers' University premises and the cinema itself, you started talking about a large number of Croat refugees from Jajce, Zenica, and other places who had lost a lot of their family and property, and they were in a terrible state because of that, and then you stopped off there. What did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation was increasingly complex. They had come frustrated from those areas. They didn't have any accommodation. I know that we gave them our holiday homes at Zabrdje, to put them up there. And their sons probably had weapons as well, that was what I heard. I cannot say for certain because I don't know about that. But they were rumours. I assume that that could have been one of the reasons. To get an apartment themselves, they expelled Muslims, or they would threaten them by phone. But -- and as I say, a portion of them left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. You have given us an answer. Mr. Lukovic, you were also asked whether you know about a place before this conflict broke out where the Croats were put up for their own safety. You said that you did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was thinking of Vitez. I was referring to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you hear whether any places of that kind existed in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to refer the Chamber to testimony of Josip Miskovic, the witness, who himself was detained as a Croat in the village of Kremenjace and held under guard in one house for his own safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a matter of comment, and you can refer to it in your final submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similarly, Mr. Lukovic, you were asked why the Muslims, or a large portion of them, left the town of Vitez, and you explained that. Do you happen to know that a large number of Croats also left Zenica, Travnik, areas where they had previously lived and areas which were predominantly inhabited by the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that. And the people from Zenica who came to Vitez, some of them were in my own work platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukovic, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Mr. Lukovic. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Our next witness is Mr. Ljubo Calic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Calic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please pull up your chair closer to the table so that we can hear you better. Thank you. Mr. Calic, on behalf of Mario Cerkez's Defence, I am going to ask you some questions, and please answer them to the best of your recollection. Also, I would point out something else to you: Can you please slow down when giving answers because everything needs to be interpreted. Can you first state your full name, date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: My name is Ljubo Calic. I was born on the 1st of August, 1960, in Nadioci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Calic, you're of Croat ethnic background and you're a Roman Catholic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're a citizen of both the BiH and the Republic of Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You graduated from the vocational school in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have your own private business and you own a coffee bar in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you serve and when, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: In Slavonska Pozega and then in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you conferred any rank in the army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Calic, could you tell us, you said that you owned this coffee bar. Since when have you owned it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Since 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this coffee bar, Macao, did it exist even before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that an explosive device was detonated there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Calic, you told us that you were born in the village of Nadioci. The Trial Chamber is fully aware of the topography of the place and they know where Nadioci is. Your parents died before the war had broken out in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But your brothers and their families live in Nadioci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also have a hobby; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a hunter.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a member of any hunting club?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you become a member of this club?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the Kruscica Hunting Club, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also get a hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to acquire a hunting rifle, you first needed to secure a permit from the authorities.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you received such a permit.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many members did the Kruscica Hunting Club have?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: I believe about 120.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall in the year before the war in 1992, who was the president of this hunting club?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Anto Krizanac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also had deputies, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Slavko Mlakic and Mirko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Calic, where did you go hunting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: It was around the town of Vitez and the area of Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I assume you often went to those areas, you roamed there, Kruscica and the mountainous terrain beyond it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area of Zabrdje is also part of that area.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a lodge there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a pretty dominant feature in reference to the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 the JNA and the Bosnian Serbs attacked Bosnia. When this happened, what happened to you who were members of this hunting club? Did you get organised?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes, we organised guards and reconnaissance. We tried to protect the lodge, this climber's lodge. And the first air raid came right over this lodge, and after that the hunters tried to organise themselves in order to protect the lodge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that area you organised yourself in order to conduct reconnaissance and potentially defend the area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was because of that JNA air raid in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Calic, these groups of yours that gathered up there, how were they organised? How many people were there in each group?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: We had shifts of seven days every month for reconnaissance, and a shift consisted of approximately 20 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was involved in these shifts?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: There were commanders, Anto Krizanac, Slavko Mlakic, and Mirko Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pavelic. They assigned people to each group, and out of these people somebody would not show, so the groups varied from 15 to 20 members of the hunting club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Calic: Did these shifts of 15 to 20 men, where did they stay the night? In that lodge?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you patrolled the terrain, the area and conducted your reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were armed with your hunting weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any radio link communication with the town?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had a radio transmitter in the lodge, and the commander maintained communication with the town. My commander was Anto Krizanac and he was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the communications centre that you were in touch with was located in the post office building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start going to these shifts at Zabrdje?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: I believe that I started in August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you kept going there until the break of hostilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider yourself a soldier when you were on these shifts or did you consider yourself a member of the hunting club?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: I was just a hunter. I was never a soldier. And I did this on behalf of the hunting club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Calic, whether someone issued an order to your hunting club to organise these groups and these shifts?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: No. The hunting club wanted to give its own contribution, and from what I know, Anto Krizanac took it upon himself to give this kind of contribution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Calic, you said that these groups were active from the latter part of 1992, but do you recall whether you were in the shift on the day when the conflict broke out, on 16 April 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall how many days before the outbreak of hostilities were you there in the shift?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to go the following day; in other words, before the conflict broke out, I was already there for five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, the day before the conflict broke out -- that is, on the 15th of April -- do you recall what you did on that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: As all other days, we went to an area called Poljana, above the lodge, and our task was to reconnoitre because we -- there was a potential danger of a helicopter attack, and this helicopter would land in this area called Poljana, or field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you called Poljana is really a plateau at Zabrdje?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that terrain was suitable for a helicopter landing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what I understood you to say, you were told that a helicopter attack would have been possible from there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, which army would have been capable of carrying out such an attack?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, on the 15th of April, your patrolling was exclusively directed against a potential attack by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told that an attack of the ABiH was also possible?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, is the water reservoir Ilidza nearby?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: It is somewhere to the left of the lodge. If you look from the town itself towards the lodge, it would be to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this reservoir used by the town of Vitez for their water supply?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said that on that day you were doing your reconnaissance -- you were on your reconnaissance duty at Poljana and then you came back to the lodge.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you stayed in the lodge?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes. After we came back from the patrol, we had a meal, and then we spent the night in the lodge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: I was awakened by explosions. That was nothing unusual, because we had been awakened by explosions before. However, I heard repeated explosions, and that was not usual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. You mentioned that you had been awakened before from explosions. From where did these explosions come, the sounds?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: They were coming from Mount Vlasic and they were shelling Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At first you thought that they were the same type of explosions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, later you realised that it was not the same?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was different?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: The difference was that the explosions were more frequent, and in earlier cases there would be five or six explosions. However, that morning the explosions continued, and I stepped out of my room to the balcony and I -- it overlooked the town. I saw that it was -- that there were fires. I was confused. I came back and I said something was wrong, this is a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. From the balcony of your room on the mountain lodge, you can see the town?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Calic, in your estimate, what is the distance, as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: I believe that it is about 3.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came out to the balcony, you saw that houses were on fire in town?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went back in to wake up your fellow hunters from the shift?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: We quickly got up, got dressed, and we started shouting, "Something's wrong. There's a war." I remember we came down and we ran into Anto Krizanac in the hallway and we told him what was going on. He looked lost and he said that he didn't know anything. He got into the room where his radio transmitter was. We had already gotten out. Then he joined us outside and he said, "The war has broken out with the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you assumed that Mr. Krizanac, who went into the radio room, you assumed that he called someone?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this radio communication still -- was it still operative that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the day, but in the evening we lost it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Krizanac tell you after he came out of the room where the radio transmitter was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: He said that the Muslims had attacked and that we had to stay there and continue to watch. He deployed us. There are a number of weekend houses around the lodge, and this is where we went and stayed there for the rest of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next? You continued to do your reconnaissance duties and to observe?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two or three went to reconnoitre and the rest of us were all deployed around the lodge where those weekend houses are, and this is where we circulated, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this reconnaissance and while you observed the terrain that day, did you observe anything?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Nothing on that first day, but on the second day I was on a reconnaissance duty with another three members. We came across two ABiH soldiers who were asleep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: That was above the village of Bobasi, at Zabrdje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who populates this village of Bobasi, predominantly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that these two soldiers were in a forest above the village, asleep?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where were they sleeping?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Next to some beech trees. They both had rifles with rocket-propelled grenades and RBs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you took them prisoner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: When I approached them, I saw ABiH insignia on their jackets. I was confused. That was the first encounter of this kind that I had. I didn't know what to do, whether to go forward or to pull back. When I almost approached one soldier, I -- it was only then that I saw the second soldier, and then I thought, well, who knows how many there are. Then I asked my colleagues to approach the other one, and that's when we took them prisoner. We made noise, and the others who were around started shooting at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that there were soldiers in the forest.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were other ABiH soldiers who were in the forest below them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the two soldiers tell you on that occasion? Did they identify themselves? Did they tell you who they were and what they were doing there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: When we took them prisoner and we started interviewing them, questioning them, they said that they were from Pezici and Kovacevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said villages of Pezici and Kovacevac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who lives predominantly in those villages?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they say? Members of which unit or which army were they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: They said they were anti-armour unit which numbered 80 men and they were stationed in Kruscica under the command of Hakija Dzelilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this unit deployed? What did they say?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: They said that the unit was deployed in Kruscica and that six soldiers were assigned there. In case of any movements, that is, in case any vehicles approached it, they were to destroy it. But I don't know where the other members of their unit were deployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Did they tell you that their task was to fight a potential attack by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But against whom?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: They said that their task was that if there was any movement from the direction of Bobasi, in a vehicle, that is, that their task was to destroy that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Bobasi was a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said that fire was opened on you from the forest?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anybody injured?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do then with the two ABiH army soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: We brought them to Zabrdje, and two hunters from the village of Veceriska took them to the village of Veceriska, where they turned them over to the village guards. That is what I assumed that they did. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this event which you just related, when did this happen? What time of the day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Later on that day, in the course of the evening or night, were there any combat operations in that location, the location of Zabrdje, where you were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Not that day, but the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: The next day we were also deployed around the lodge in that area, and one of the hunters noticed camouflage uniforms with white ribbons, and he saw them taking shelter from tree to tree. And then we heard "Allah-u-ekber" and there was intense fire. We all pulled out and pulled back to the village of Veceriska. When we reached an area about 500 metres away from the lodge, only six of us gathered, and we did not know what had happened to the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here, Mr. Calic. What you are just relating, it could have happened on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you're saying, it is clear that you were attacked.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who attacked you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: At that moment we did not know exactly who it was, but when the first shouts were heard and when the first shouts were heard [as interpreted], when this man Ceko said, "There are people moving," when he jumped up, the fire was opened, and I believe that that was some heavier weapons. We took positions and answered fire, and then we retreated under fire. Then we heard the shouts "Allah-u-ekber," "Allah-u-ekber," and then Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it was clear to us what was going on. Then there were explosions that shook the whole lodge. When the second projectile hit the lodge, it started fire. Then we retreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So the lodge was attacked by small-arms fire and, you said, some heavier weapon and some grenades.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the lodge caught fire.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Meanwhile, you retreated and you started downhill through the forest, in the direction of a village. What village?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: The village of Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the six of you eventually gathered.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were 13 in your group. Where were the others?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: No one knew where the others were. The six of us somehow gathered during this retreat, and we stopped on the mountain path and we said, "Maybe we should stop and wait to see whether we'll be joined by any others."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody arrived?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: We heard through the forest that somebody was coming down, and we called out and they responded. One by one they came. Anto Krizanac, the commander, had a leg injury; I believe that one of the hunters helped him out. We all came over to see him and he said, "Just take positions. Everything is going to be all right."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Out of the 13 of you, Mr. Anto Krizanac was injured.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anybody else injured?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Several minutes later we heard more noises of somebody coming down through the forest. Zeljo Bevanda brought this man Ceko. His eye was knocked out, and I believe he also had a leg injury.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you went down to the village of Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes, we went down to the village of Veceriska. The locals said that we couldn't stay there, that we had to go back and protect that position. We then turned around and we were joined by these locals from the village, and we went back towards the lodge. It took us all night to get up there, and at the break of dawn we arrived at the lodge, which had been burned down and abandoned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question before we break. When the villagers said that the village was endangered, what did they mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: They said they meant that the ABiH would come and that we had to protect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this may be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll adjourn now. Mr. Calic, we're going to adjourn for a break for half an hour. During the break could you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over and not to let anybody speak to you about it. We'll adjourn now until half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Calic, I believe we can move on. Before the adjournment you told us that that night slowly, with the village guards in Veceriska, you climbed the mountain, reached the mountaineer's lodge and saw that it had been abandoned and that it had burned down.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: With the help of villagers from Gornja Veceriska, we all deployed from the lodge to the summer cottages, because down there were quite a number of them, and that is where we took our positions and remained surveying the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at Zabrdje?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: I stayed at Zabrdje until the late afternoon of the 20th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went where?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: On the 20th, late in the afternoon, with Ilija Maric and Tonci Kadinovic, I went down to the village of Bobasi slowly; and from Bobasi via Gradina I went to Vitez, to my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then eventually go to the village where you were born, to Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: On the night of the 20th [as interpreted], when I arrived there my family already thought that I had been killed, because you can see from our flat the mountaineer's lodge and they could see the flames and heard the attack. My wife and children thought that I had been killed, and they were very happy but very confused when I arrived, and everybody was crying. But that night I spent in the cellar in my building, and together with me there were other tenants in the same building. There is a ground floor and two stories, and we all spent that night in the cellar sleeping on some boards and things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in point of fact, it was an improvised shelter there, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: The next day, when I got up I went to Slavko Mlakic's house. He was the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The deputy commander of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Of the hunting unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. The hunting unit.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask him did he know what had happened to Anto Krizanac and Zeljo Bevanda who had been wounded. And when I came home, my wife told me where he was, because I knew nothing at all. His wife told me that he was at Gradina. Gradina is above the town of Vitez, right above it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Later on, Mr. Calic, did you go to your native village, to Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: In the evening of the 20th of April I went to my native village of Nadioci for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the village of Nadioci, I went to the place called Krc straight away. Village guards were there, or rather all the people from my native people - most of them, not all of them - but most of them were up there on duty in that woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to correct the record. Page 40, line 9, it says the 20th of April rather than the 24th of April as the day when you arrived in the village of Nadioci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the locality of Krc where the villagers from Nadioci were, that is, members of the village guards from Nadioci. Where is the place called Krc in relation to Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: The place called Krc is between Nadioci and the village of Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far from the village of Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: About a kilometre and a half, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A defence line had been established there, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived on the 24th, did you already find there an established line and trenches?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: When I arrived, yes, there were some trenches but very few. But since it is a wood there, mostly trees were used, and a few dug trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you expect a possible attack of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: From the direction of Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who commanded the village guards in Nadioci at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: At that time when I arrived, the village guards were commanded by Zdravko Calic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came, were the village guards already incorporated in one way or another in a military unit, in the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: All I could see was that it was incorporated in the defence of the village, just as I had come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, who was your immediate superior at that locality?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: When I came there, my immediate superior at that locality was Slavko Papic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your duty?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: When I came there, the very next day in the evening I was together with those men. We dug trenches a little. In the morning Slavko Papic came and told me to command that area together with Drago Calic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Slavko Papic; will you tell us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Slavko Papic was the commander of that sector. As I said, I didn't know much about it, but he told me he was the sector commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was the one who issued orders to you, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your chief task there? How did he explain it to you? What were you to do at that place, Krc?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't have to explain to us a great deal because we knew even without him that we had to dig in. And our only task was to protect our native village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any attacks on your defence line at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Repeatedly, or just one? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Those attacks meant gunfire, but until the 25th of May there was nothing serious. There would only be gunfire from the direction of Vrhovine. It was only on the 25th of May that a fierce attack took place. They broke through our lines. Srecko Botic, who was right next to me, was killed, and not far from me, the late Slavko Papic was also there and he was killed that same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that day, on the 25th of May, 1993, you remember a fierce attack on your positions, do you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What forces were used for the attack?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: There was shelling and an infantry attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned those two, Slavko Papic, who was the commander, and who was killed that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, what happened then? Did you manage to reject the attack or did you have to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: That first day we managed to reject the attack -- that is, some trenches were taken away -- and late that same day we managed to recover those same trenches. Five men were killed that day. I don't know how many wounded. Quite a number of them were wounded. And late that day we managed to recover those trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you function then, when your commander, Slavko Papic, was killed? Who took over his duty?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: When Slavko Papic was killed, Anto Bertovic, the commander, came and told me that I had to take over that whole sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your summary, it says that it was Marko Cerkez who came. Are you sure? Was it Anto Bertovic or Marko Cerkez who came?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was Anto Bertovic, and he told me that Mario Cerkez and he had talked and agreed that I should be the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as of that day, you took over the post of the commander, did you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO CALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall ask you to look at a document, Mr. Calic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D124/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
