utterances.text: The armed Muslims, most of them, left the village, along with the -- along the SPS fence. Some of them stayed on. They surrendered their weapons. And the civilians, women, children, and the elderly, were left there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to those civilians, the civilians who stayed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I was on the opposite side of the line. I don't know how to explain this to you. They were taken into town and were returned several hours later. Allegedly, they had been taken off by the Vitezovi, but I did not see that because I was on the other side. And also during the conflict, when the conflict broke out, I took some of the Muslims to our first aid centre, medical centre, for safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that there was any abuse of these civilians that were taken to town and brought back again?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know after it was all over how many wounded there were in Gacice, and on what side? I mean who did these victims belong to?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I don't have the facts about this, but there were injured people, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there wounded on both sides?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were wounded on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, for the record, please, the two wounded individuals who you took to the doctor in Vitez. One was Fadil Hrustic and the other? And the other?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Teufik Subasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew both of them personally, did you not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Teufik went to school with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it easy for you to take those people there? Was it an easy assignment?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No. It was very difficult. But as I knew them personally and they weren't bad people, they were good neighbours, I took it upon myself to take them, to help these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were taking them to the village, you had a problem with an UNPROFOR transporter; is that right? What happened?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: At the exit to the village of Mlakici, the road is very narrow, there are fences on both sides, and they wouldn't let me go by. But as I know the village - I was born there and lived there - I took a byroad and was able to take them to where they were going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened to the Muslim civilians when they were returned to Gacice? Do you happen to know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they put up?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: They were accommodated in about ten houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did it happen that way?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Well, there were some houses which were not destroyed and they could stay there. But to ensure their own safety -- what I want to say is this: The situation was such that right next to us was the battlefield, Kruscica, the Muslims, and the Mahala just divided by the field. So for their safety, and safety for our own people, our own soldiers as well, to protect them, because these soldiers might have been ready to take some diversionary activity. So it was purely to protect their lives. They had everything they needed. Let me tell you, we didn't have enough soldiers to cover the line, but we did set aside a certain portion nonetheless to guard these people, to look after them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to those people that were put up in those ten houses, any bad things?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No. I would never wish for a situation like that. But if a situation like that did arise again, then I hope that people would behave towards me as I behaved towards them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mlakic, did you feel responsible for the safety of those people?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that if something were to happen to them, it would happen to you as well one day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mlakic, at one given point since the beginning of the war, you became a member, not only you but your neighbours as well, you became members of the village guards, and other mobilised men too; and you became members of the Vitez Brigade as well at one point; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that occurred? And how were you able to determine that as of one particular moment you were members of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Well, the number of people that took part in the village guards, they were not soldiers, these people, they were just ordinary villagers who stood guard to defend their houses. After the mobilisation was proclaimed, and I can't tell you the exact date, all the available men were mobilised, all the military-abled men, able-bodied men. This was done on the basis of lists. I made up the lists as well and sent them to the command during the course of the war; I know that I did make a list of the able-bodied men who could be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one day you were asked to provide a list of the military-able men from the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that took place? A day after the conflict, two, five, ten days? What period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was three or four days later, maybe five days later. But it was at least three or four days after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mlakic, who told you to make up the lists?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: The command, the command of the Vitez Brigade, the then Vitez Brigade. They wanted to sound out the situation in Vitez municipality. Whether it came from them directly or the statistics department for military-able men, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You as a member of the village guard, were you asked this before the 16th of April? Did a request of that kind come to you before that date?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The record states the statistics department. What institution did you have in mind when you talked about statistics?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No. I mean the department -- the people who at the beginning of the conflict wanted to see how many able-bodied men there were for the army. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember what that department or office was called?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that it actually existed. But that's what I meant. I meant these people, these people who wanted to know how many military-able men there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So it was that day when you received this request and complied that you had actually become mobilised soldiers, as of that date.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do consider that. But we weren't soldiers straight away. First of all, we didn't have any weapons. We knew nothing about war. So we weren't really soldiers straight away, and it is debatable whether we actually ever became soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the days that followed were you given any concrete orders from the command of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: First of all, for the purposes of ensuring protection for the village. We were afraid of an attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you military orders of any kind at that time? The name and surname, in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't hear from Mario much in the war, in those first days of the war. We heard nothing from him. Maybe a month later I received -- I can't say exactly. I received some orders, but they all referred to defence; to reinforce the guards, to take steps to secure defence and safety, to keep awake and alert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mario. Do you mean Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive orders from Ivica Drmic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, from Ivica Drmic, because Ivica Drmic was the commander of a sector. The area was divided up into sectors at the time, and Mario Cerkez as the commander of the Vitez Brigade probably issued orders to Ivica Drmic, and in his turn Ivica Drmic relayed those orders to me, down the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mlakic, during those days, did you personally, or your men, receive any documents, pieces of paper, which said, "You are mobilised and assigned to such and such a position," or anything like that, any similar piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. I can't remember. There were some sort of certificates as to affiliation in the brigade, membership in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they issue certificates then, or were they issued later on?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: They started being issued sometime in August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Mr. Mlakic, do you agree that you gradually became soldiers, but that you yourself cannot set an actual date as to when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. May I just take a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should like to show the witness a certificate from another village and ask him whether he received a similar certificate. May I have D121/2, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mlakic, we're going to show you a certificate which did not relate to your area. But just tell us whether you ever saw a similar certificate, or perhaps received a certificate like that one, if you remember. If you do, say yes; if not, tell us. Did you receive certificates like this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Possibly, yes. I think that I might have a similar one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you received it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I see that the date here is May. Well, perhaps I got mine in June or July, but not before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you couldn't find a certificate like this in your house.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as written documents are concerned, I don't really know exactly. And I moved houses, I built a new house and moved, so some of the papers might have been left behind. It's difficult to say. But when I see the certificate, it reminds me of my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the war progressed, from the defence of the sector you moved to another organisational form. Could you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Well, the defence of the sector were the village guards at the beginning of the war. Later on there was more military-type organisation; companies, platoons, battalions, all that began to be established. So that I became part of the 4th Company of the 4th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any official appointment?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I received any official appointment. It was the status quo, as it was before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was your job, in fact?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I was the commander of a company at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in that same position, the same locality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same positions, the same locality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as your military obligation was concerned, did anything change?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Nothing changed. Just that piece of paper, which I'm not quite sure whether I ever got it or not. But that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this transition to this other type of organisation, that happened in the early summer, did it not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to this change in organisation and establishment, do you remember whether in the early autumn another reorganisation took place?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. When Bobasi fell, the situation was critical for the Vitez area and the SPS factory, and the secondary organisation took place for defence, which means that the sectors were organised again and new commanders took charge of the sectors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sector did you belong to at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: The third sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of that sector was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Ilija Nakic. And the commander of the fourth sector, next to me, was Mr. Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that at that time Mario Cerkez played the same role that you had in your sector; in another sector, that Cerkez was subordinate --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No. Mario Cerkez was the commander of a sector, and I was alongside the commander, that is to say, underneath the commander who was Ilija Nakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these sectors, did they have their areas of responsibility strictly defined?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were defined in spatial terms. There was the first, second, and third area of responsibility and sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Each of these sectors were part of the line around the Vitez pocket; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mine was three kilometres and 500 metres, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over this stretch of three or four kilometres which was your sector, how many men did you have?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Very few to begin with, until Bobasi fell. About 20 or 30 people. But with the fall of Bobasi, the number of men increased; they came from other lines as reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To avoid any misunderstanding, the ethnic composition, what was the village of Bobasi?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Bobasi had a mixed population, Croats and Muslims together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who had to retreat from Bobasi when Bobasi fell?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: The Croats did, because Bobasi was taken over by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Cerkez at that time, at the beginning of the autumn, was commander of the sector next door to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know how far his sector stretched?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say exactly, but it was about the same size as my own. It wasn't smaller than mine. So it was -- he covered a substantial portion of the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Like your sector, more or less; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mlakic, tell us, please: Did you at any time during that unfortunate war, were you involved in any military operations except in the area of your village and lines in the vicinity of your village?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you wounded during the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 30th of December, 1993 -- 13th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 30th, the day before the New Year?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and I was taken to the hospital in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have been proclaimed an invalid?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am an invalid 20 per cent. I received a wound in my leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were wounded, you were a member of the Vitez Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of this 92nd Home Guard Regiment?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but at the end of the war with the Muslims, I took people to the Kupres lines, the lines facing -- the front line facing the Serbs, and then I was a member at that time of the 92nd Home Guard Regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when the regiment was established?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us roughly.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: After the war, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean after the Washington agreements?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the Kupres operation and so on. Just to make things clear, they were military operations after the Washington agreements, where Croatia and the forces of the BH army went together to liberate the southern stretches of Bosnia from the JNA, the army of Republika Srpska from the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you demobilised?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I returned to the same job I had before the conflict with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you became a civilian, or did you continue to perform this job within the frameworks of your wartime assignment?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I was a civilian, but I was still in the 92nd Home Guard Regiment organisation, which organised its members along the defence line facing the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mlakic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no questions for Mr. Mlakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, one map, three documents, and I'll try and accommodate the timetable just by being very selective. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first speak to lawyers about the evidence you've given, please, Mr. Mlakic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: The first time I talked, a year ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: About a year ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this summary that's been served on us prepared first? When was the first draft of it prepared?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a chance yesterday, or some days ago, to go through the summary that's been served on us and to satisfy yourself that it was accurate?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Well, what I gave and what I listened to, what the lawyers told me, if that's the summary, then I agree; it's all correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you tried to set out there everything that was important? Yes?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps there are some other things too the lawyer didn't ask me. Maybe there are some other important things that I didn't mention there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The map, for help, which is D88/2 or Z2160. You may not have seen this map before. You'll be shown by the usher how to point to things. It's quite detailed. And if we focus in to the south-west of Vitez -- south-west, sorry. Over a bit. Other way. There we are. Does this show us the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Could you move the map up a bit? Mlakici are [as interpreted] underneath Gacice and Ocice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just point out where you were living? Point it out on the overhead projector. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: That's Vitez, Gacice, Lupnica, Rijeka, the river running through Nakic. This is where Mlakici is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So that is not only less than a kilometre; it's less than half a kilometre from the centre of Vitez, correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: About half a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You tell us that some anti-aircraft guns were taken -- was it by one man with a horse and cart, to Stari Vitez? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No. I can't say it was one man. But we were told that that man organised the transport of those guns. His name was Djuda, with a cart, but he couldn't transport three guns. It was raining, and they took advantage of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this taking of the anti-aircraft guns the subject of any written record or complaint anywhere, Mr. Mlakic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Probably no written complaints by me and those in Mlakici, but the fact is that those guns were our joint property; they were ours and they were the Muslims as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... question on this topic. You're now saying, you see, to the Judges that this could have happened as early as 1992, before any real conflict, it may be thought, broke out between Muslims and Croats. In your summary you said 1993. Are you really suggesting that the Muslims took anti-aircraft guns, without complaint and without an issue arising out of it, in 1992? Are you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I said that I'm not sure whether it was the beginning of 1993 or the end of 1992. So it was in that period, thereabouts, either the end of 1992 or the beginning of 1993. But that was the period. I'm not quite certain of the date, but that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to put these events in 1992, Mr. Mlakic. Are you trying to paint the picture more black for the Muslims than, on any reckoning, it ever was? Is that what you're trying to do?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document, first of three, Z653, usual performance. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at this document. The English will go on the overhead projector. Let me just remind you of some of the evidence that's emerged this afternoon. The following question was put to you. Before you look at the document, Mr. Mlakic, just listen to me. The following question was put to you by counsel: "Do you agree you gradually became a soldier but can't say a date?" to which you gave your assent. Look, please, at this document. This is a document dated before the conflict, on the 14th of April. It comes from the Viteska Brigade. It identifies, for Kamenjace and Gacice, 12 and 5 soldiers, respectively, because they are personnel of the 1st Battalion of the Viteska Brigade, the 3rd Company, under the man of Ivica Drmic, who was, on any account, to become, if he wasn't already, your commander. Can you explain, please, for us the presence of that number of military personnel in your village before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I see the figures 12 and 5. They were soldiers who lived in Mlakici, that's true, in Kamenjace and Gacice, to be exact. But they were soldiers. They weren't the village guards. That means they were soldiers who did shifts facing, on the line facing the Serbs. And they would be 7, 10, 3, depending how many days, and then would go back home, and then they were free. Some worked in companies. So those were those soldiers, that's true, but these are not the people who were in the village guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were soldiers under the command of Cerkez in your village before the conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: They were under the command of Ivica Drmic, and they did shifts on the line facing the Serbs, which means to Vlasic and two or three other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher would be good enough to place the plan back on the ELMO. We may need it just once more. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The night of the 15th, 16th, is my next topic. We can focus again, just to remind ourselves of the location of the -- that's fine like, that. Absolutely fine. Perhaps a little bit closer in so that we can -- but not too much, because we now know where you are. You are really just on the corner of those roads to the west of Vitez, and a kilometre or so from the body of the SPS factory to the west; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: You mean the place where I lived, whether I was there that night?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Between the 15th and the 16th?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that the evening was entirely uneventful. I want you to think back, please. What time did you go to bed on the night of the 15th?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much you listened while I was talking to the Defence counsel, that I was moving things into the new house, because on the next day I was to have a little celebration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was listening. It's a simple question. We're pressed for time. What time, if at all, did you go to bed on the night of the 15th, 16th?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I did not go to sleep, because I went down to the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Whereabouts was the command? Show us on the map.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: The village command was in a house. It was not a regular -- we just called it that. This is where we would make schedules for the village guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stayed awake all night?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you first aware of the Vitezovi being present in the centre of Vitez and in your part of the suburbs so close to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I said that I saw a group of soldiers passing through Mlakici, and I realised that these were Vitezovi when I recognised a man who was with the Vitezovi --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: -- and who was very close to our trenches. It was on the same day, the 16th. I don't know what time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: On the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you not aware of them being present there from sometime in the middle of the night, securing the centre of Vitez and probably your suburb as well?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because I'm going to suggest to you that following a plan to go and attack the Muslims that night, the Vitezovi were charged with looking after the centre of town, and that's why eventually they came out on your road towards the factory. Now, were you aware of them there in the centre of town that night?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw them the following day, did they have ribbons on their arms, distinctive coloured ribbons?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall, because we saw them from a distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to the 16th, please. You, of course -- just let me ask you: Were you aware on the 16th that the HVO generally was attacking and mounting an all-out attack on the Muslims that morning? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No. General chaos. I don't know who was attacking whom. The shells were falling, the bullets were whizzing by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I wanted your help with. You told us earlier, "Shells were falling on us." Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. On our village, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When? What time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out, when the shooting started, then those shells started falling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Try and give us an approximate time, if you can, please, for the time when shells were falling on your village. I'm sorry about the pronunciation. Kamenjace, shells falling on Kamenjace. Tell us, please: When was it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, this is the first time that something like this happened to us, or to me. I cannot tell you exactly when, but I know that that day looked like an eternity. I cannot place it in time. I cannot say they fell at such-and-such an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put one possibility to you and see what you say. Isn't the truth of the matter that there was an early morning attack, perhaps elsewhere from where you were, and there was no question of shells landing on your particular part of Vitez until very much later, and that was by way of reaction, but it was much later. Now, do you accept that? If so, we'll move on. Or do you reject that and say that shells landed on your part of Vitez right at the beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: The shells started falling in the morning, so the conflict started in the morning. I cannot say that they started immediately but they started falling later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You see, in your summary, which I've read and which you can have in front of you, of course, if you want to, what you said was this, you said: "I saw grenades falling on Vitez and shooting around Stari Vitez," paragraph 2.6. You spoke of chaos and confusion and of a sniper bullet attack and matters of that sort. But you say: "In our village there was no conflict," paragraph 2.8. Unless I've missed it - I'll be corrected, of course, if I'm wrong - no where in your summary do you suggest that shells were falling on your part of the village at that time of the morning, because they weren't, were they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No, that is the summary. I'm trying to explain certain things. And what I said, I stand by it. It is true that the shells did fall in Vitez, but also they fell on Mlakici and Kamenjace. The sniper was operating from Mahala; I don't know exactly from where. But I know that a man in Mlakici was wounded by a sniper bullet coming from Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you, Mr. Mlakic, that that's quite wrong and that the difference between what your account is and your summary shows that you're trying to embellish the history in a way that you believe to be favourable; do you follow the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your first name, is there anybody else with the same first name as you in the village of Mlakici, or are you the only Nikola Mlakic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: There are several Nikola Mlakics in Mlakici, and there are several other persons by the name of Nikola Mlakic in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your area, in your suburb, there's a man called Ivka Mlakic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Ivka Mlakic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or Karlo Mlakic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: There is Karlo. But Ivka Malkic would be a woman, not a man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. My mistake. Do you know her house?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Ivka Mlakic's house is closer to Vitez than to Mlakici. It is on the outskirts of Mlakici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that on the morning of the 16th of April of 1993 a multiple rocket launcher was positioned in the gardens of both those houses, one after the other, and used to fire on Stari Vitez, or the Mahala, as it's called; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I have no such information, and I believe it is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you saying that it would be possible, given the small scale of this suburb, for a multiple rocket launcher to be used in that area and for you not to know about it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I don't believe it was used, that multiple rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The factory that lies so close to your village, was that known to contain acid and fuel in large quantities at the time of the outbreak of the fighting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, was it clear to you that the Vitezovi were going there to secure the factory, or doing their best to secure the factory?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I heard that several days later, when they explained why they were passing through the morning we saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Gacice, very briefly. The upshot of Gacice was that a number of people, Muslims, were taken away and imprisoned; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No, not imprisoned. But a number of people were taken and brought back immediately, several hours later. And later those able-bodied men, some of them, that is, were taken for protection either in the cinema theatre or somewhere else. I don't know where. But they were moved there for their own protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the attack on the occupants of Gacice, is it right, as we've heard from another Defence witness - the page reference is 24316 - that involved in that attack were 20 village guards, 10 or 15 Vitezovi, members of the police, and some villagers from your village, from Mlakici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: First you said "the attack." I would rather call it the defence. This was to protect the Croats in Gacice. So it was a defence rather than an attack. It was to provide assistance to the men who were outnumbered by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the upshot of it all was that the Muslims were sent packing and the place was retained by the Croats, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No, they were not sent packing. The Muslims stayed, as I said, in about ten houses which were secured, protected, by these Croat village guards. And they were free to go whenever they wished to rejoin their families or the able-bodied men who had left that village that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Muslim areas, they would have been free to go, would they? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were free to go to Muslim areas; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll use my version for speed; 742.3, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document, you see, dated the 20th of April. You don't have to look. It's from the Viteska Brigade, goes to the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. Just as to Gacice, it says this: "The Gacice village is 100% completed. 47 men were taken prisoner. Women and children were sent home." Does that agree with your recollection, thinking back now?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Women and children were taken back home, that is true. And 47 men, I don't recall whether there were 47. The able-bodied men were taken -- they were not imprisoned, they were not tied, they were not forcibly removed. They were taken to either the school building or the cinema building. I cannot tell you exactly where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area was cleansed, wasn't it, Gacice, eventually?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "cleansed." You mean ethnically cleansed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: A few Muslims stayed; they were right next to the Gacice village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A new document, the last of the documents I'm going to put to this witness, 694.3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document, Mr. Mlakic, that we have, you'll see, from Darko Kraljevic of the Vitezovi, and you've told us about the Vitezovi operating in your area. This is dated the 17th of April, and it goes to the head of the defence, Bruno Stojic, and the forward command post and says this: "We have managed to clear a large part of the city of the dastardly Muslim forces and I am constantly attacking! Their strongest stronghold is where their headquarters are - north-western suburbs. At the same time, we are engaged in the front ranks in the cleaning of the surrounding villages and interventions to reclaim the lines we lost." And then it deals with Vitezovi killed and ammunition. Does this describe the true position that was going on there, because you were in the west or north-west of Vitez, that they were engaged in the front ranks in cleaning the surrounding villages? Is that what was going on?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I cannot say that because I was preoccupied by the protection of my village. The PPN Vitezovi were not in contact with me, so I cannot say anything. As regards his reporting to Stojic, that was his business because he was the commander of the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must suggest to you that you know perfectly well from your proximity to the centre of Vitez - if you didn't know it on the night, you must have heard it subsequently - that there was an all-out attack on the Muslims that night, and what happened in Gacice and thereabouts was all part of a consistent plan; that's the truth, isn't it, Mr. Mlakic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I would like to request, sir, can you explain to me how could I have known when there were no operations there? You mean the night between the 15th and the 16th?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Between the night of the 15th and 16th, you know that there was going to be an all-out attack which took place on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: It's something else, "should have," because you said that there was an attack. According to you, it should have happened. But that night was fairly calm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, two other things, very brief. You said something about Stari Vitez. Stari Vitez was being attacked, wasn't it, from an early stage on the 16th? Or the Mahala, if that's the better way to describe it.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether Stari Vitez was attacked. I said that I knew what I received from Mahala, Stari Vitez, which was sniper fire, because I was in Mlakici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stari Vitez was an area occupied by Muslims who were defending themselves from the 16th of April onwards, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Correct, but not all of Stari Vitez. Only a part of Stari Vitez was held by the Muslims; the other part was held by the Croats. So Muslims held one part of Stari Vitez, and they were there in the Mahala throughout that war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were protecting themselves from Croats who were attacking them. It's quite simple and it's quite obvious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way, because I don't know from which side they were attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mlakic, you were pretty close, and you're telling us that effectively you were very close, in your summary. There's no question of the people of Stari Vitez trying to take over Vitez, is there? They were simply defending themselves from those who were attacking them; that's why I suggested to you it makes sense; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Sir, can I give you an example of the situation to show you that it wasn't like that? If somebody on the front line would fire, the whole line would start to shoot. And the Muslims started shooting from all their weapons, and then it would turn out that nobody was attacking anybody else but everybody was shooting. So they thought that we were attacking them, they thought that we were going to attack them, and the other way around. So each side would think that they were about to be attacked by the other side, as if Mlakici were attacking Stari Vitez or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have heard from Marijan Strukar that he was warned in advance about the truck bomb. Somebody came and told him in your area about the truck bomb that was going to blow up. Do you remember being warned about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No. We heard a loud explosion. We couldn't see what the blast was about, and there had been several blasts before so we didn't know what it was. Later on we learned that it was a car bomb which had exploded in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, you're suggesting that Cerkez was in some position other than a brigade commander. I must suggest to you, and there are documents by the plenty to prove it, that he was a brigade commander and giving instructions as a brigade commander until the end of December 1993; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say that he was not the brigade commander. He was the brigade commander. But I most probably was in touch with Ivica Drmic, who was his subordinate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'll be very, very brief. Re-examined by Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mlakic, can you tell the Trial Chamber, when did you arrive in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I arrived in The Hague Tuesday night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This week? Tuesday of this week?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Tuesday of this week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mlakic, how much sleep did you have Tuesday to Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: About two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I was sick when I started out. I wanted to come and help the people who are here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you meet me regarding this summary? Can you orient yourself in that time period?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: It definitely was not on that day. We met the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that yesterday morning?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was yesterday. Things are going very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I ask you about some other things after you signed this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point during your examination, my learned colleague suggested to you or put to you that you, Mr. Mlakic, are trying to embellish the history - that was page 105, line 6 - and you said yes as to whether you understood what the suggestion was. Does that mean that you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No. I said that I understood what he asked me but that I did not agree. So that no, the answer was no, I did not agree to what he suggested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you understood what he was suggesting to you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I confirmed that I understood the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'm a bit fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection to that, by your statement, have you embellished the history, the story, or did you relay things as you saw them?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: In my statement I signed things -- I signed on the things as I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were given an operations report of the brigade and you talked to my learned colleague about it; 47 men were mentioned there. There, you said, "I know that they were taken." This came up twice, and the second time you said, "to the cinema building or the school building." Which school were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: The school in Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which HVO unit had control of the Dubravica school?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. It was the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mlakic, did anyone, before the conflict on the morning of the 16th, tell you that there would be a war on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Of course not. I would not have planned a celebration, I would not have been involved in this building of my house had I known what was to come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the edge of your village and the first houses, apart from those two houses which we mentioned out in the field, that is, between the edge of Stari Vitez, especially the section called Mahala, is a heath.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's nothing on this heath except for those two houses which we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's an open field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you call this field between these two sites?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to call it. An open field, an empty field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given that on both sides there were armed forces, would that be called an open space?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would any civilian walk about in this area?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No, of course not, because both sides would see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a civilian or a soldier would try to pass there, do you think that he would make it through alive?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: That is questionable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the morning of 16 April, did you have any information on the events in the centre of town, especially in Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MLAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mlakic, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is one matter I want to raise, which I'm going to do in closed session when the witness is withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
